claim: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are used by all free-living organisms and many viruses to catalyze an essential step in the de novo biosynthesis of DNA precursors.
source: RNRs are used by all free-living organisms and many viruses for the conversion of ribonucleotides to 2ʹ-deoxyribonucleotides in the de novo biosynthesis of DNA precursors (Torrents et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Torrents et al., 2002, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: RNRs exhibit high diversity in primary sequence and cofactor requirement.
source: RNRs are especially fascinating from an evolutionary perspective as they exhibit high diversity in primary sequence and cofactor requirement (Lundin et al., 2015), yet they share a common fold and radical-based catalytic mechanism for nucleotide reduction (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lundin et al., 2015 and Licht et al., 1996.

claim: RNRs share a common fold and radical-based catalytic mechanism for nucleotide reduction.
source: RNRs are especially fascinating from an evolutionary perspective as they exhibit high diversity in primary sequence and cofactor requirement (Lundin et al., 2015), yet they share a common fold and radical-based catalytic mechanism for nucleotide reduction (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Licht et al., 1996.

claim: The full catalytic cycle of RNRs involves three steps: cofactor-mediated generation of a thiyl radical at a conserved cysteine in the active site, nucleotide reduction, and re-reduction of the active site after turnover.
source: Based on current biochemical evidence, the full catalytic cycle is thought to involve three steps in all RNRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): cofactor-mediated generation of a thiyl radical at a conserved cysteine in the active site, nucleotide reduction, and re-reduction of the active site after turnover (Greene et al., 2020; Holmgren and Sengupta, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greene et al., 2020 and Holmgren and Sengupta, 2010, and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The core structure of the RNR catalytic subunit (α) is a conserved 10-stranded α/β barrel.
source: Despite being a diverse enzyme family, the core structure of the catalytic subunit (known as α) is a conserved 10-stranded α/β barrel with the thiyl radical on the so-called 'finger loop' which connects the two halves of the barrel (Figure 1; Uhlin and Eklund, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uhlin and Eklund, 1996, and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The thiyl radical in RNRs is located on the 'finger loop' which connects the two halves of the barrel.
source: Despite being a diverse enzyme family, the core structure of the catalytic subunit (known as α) is a conserved 10-stranded α/β barrel with the thiyl radical on the so-called 'finger loop' which connects the two halves of the barrel (Figure 1; Uhlin and Eklund, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uhlin and Eklund, 1996, and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: RNRs have been biochemically classified into three major groups based on the cofactor used to generate the thiyl radical.
source: RNRs have been biochemically classified into three major groups based on the cofactor used to generate the thiyl radical (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which illustrates the three classes and their cofactors.

claim: Class I RNRs use a ferritin subunit (β) to house a stable radical cofactor.
source: Class I RNRs use a ferritin subunit (β) to house a stable radical cofactor and are further subclassified by the metal content of the cofactor (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Ruskoski and Boal, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011, and Ruskoski and Boal, 2021.

claim: Class I RNRs are further subclassified by the metal content of the cofactor.
source: Class I RNRs use a ferritin subunit (β) to house a stable radical cofactor and are further subclassified by the metal content of the cofactor (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Ruskoski and Boal, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011, and Ruskoski and Boal, 2021.

claim: For every turnover in class I RNRs, the α and β subunits must form a complex to engage in long-range radical transfer to the active site.
source: For every turnover, the α and β subunits must form a complex to engage in long-range radical transfer to the active site (Kang et al., 2020; Seyedsayamdost et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2020, and Seyedsayamdost et al., 2007.

claim: In class II RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a 5ʹ-deoxyadenosyl radical (5ʹ-dAdo•) produced from an adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) cofactor bound within the active site.
source: In class II RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a 5ʹ-deoxyadenosyl radical (5ʹ-dAdo•) produced from an adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) cofactor bound within the active site, and thus these enzymes do not require additional subunits (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Licht et al., 1996.

claim: Class II RNRs do not require additional subunits.
source: In class II RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a 5ʹ-deoxyadenosyl radical (5ʹ-dAdo•) produced from an adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) cofactor bound within the active site, and thus these enzymes do not require additional subunits (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Licht et al., 1996.

claim: In class III RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a glycyl radical on the C-terminal domain of the α subunit.
source: In class III RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a glycyl radical on the C-terminal domain of the α subunit, which itself is generated by a separate activase enzyme that utilizes S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) bound to a [4Fe-4S] cluster for radical chemistry (Wei et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2014b.

claim: The glycyl radical in class III RNRs is generated by a separate activase enzyme that utilizes S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) bound to a [4Fe-4S] cluster for radical chemistry.
source: In class III RNRs, the thiyl radical is generated by a glycyl radical on the C-terminal domain of the α subunit, which itself is generated by a separate activase enzyme that utilizes S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) bound to a [4Fe-4S] cluster for radical chemistry (Wei et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2014b.

claim: Once the thiyl radical is produced in the active site, nucleotide reduction proceeds via a conserved mechanism for all classes.
source: Once the thiyl radical is produced in the active site, nucleotide reduction proceeds via a conserved mechanism for all classes (Licht et al., 1996; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Licht et al., 1996, and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In most RNRs, nucleotide reduction is coupled with the oxidation of a conserved pair of active-site cysteines.
source: In most RNRs, nucleotide reduction is coupled with the oxidation of a conserved pair of active-site cysteines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Booker et al., 1994; Mao et al., 1992; Wei et al., 2014a), which are ultimately reduced by a thioredoxin system to enable the next round of turnover, although some class III RNRs use formate to directly reduce the active site (Wei et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Booker et al., 1994, Mao et al., 1992, and Wei et al., 2014a, and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The oxidized active-site cysteines in RNRs are ultimately reduced by a thioredoxin system to enable the next round of turnover.
source: In most RNRs, nucleotide reduction is coupled with the oxidation of a conserved pair of active-site cysteines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Booker et al., 1994; Mao et al., 1992; Wei et al., 2014a), which are ultimately reduced by a thioredoxin system to enable the next round of turnover, although some class III RNRs use formate to directly reduce the active site (Wei et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Booker et al., 1994, Mao et al., 1992, and Wei et al., 2014a.

claim: Some class III RNRs use formate to directly reduce the active site.
source: In most RNRs, nucleotide reduction is coupled with the oxidation of a conserved pair of active-site cysteines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Booker et al., 1994; Mao et al., 1992; Wei et al., 2014a), which are ultimately reduced by a thioredoxin system to enable the next round of turnover, although some class III RNRs use formate to directly reduce the active site (Wei et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2014b.

claim: Except for a subset of class II RNRs which are monomeric, all extant RNR α subunits are thought to dimerize at the αA and αB helices in their active forms.
source: Except for a subset of class II RNRs which are monomeric, all extant RNR α subunits are thought to dimerize at the αA and αB helices in their active forms.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about RNR structure and function.

claim: Class I and II RNRs dimerize in anti-parallel orientation at the αA and αB helices.
source: Class I and II RNRs dimerize in anti-parallel orientation at these helices, such that the dimer interface is capped on both ends with a functional insertion known as loop 1 (Figure 1B–C, dark green), which is the binding site for nucleotides that control the identity of the substrate in the active site (Larsson et al., 2004; Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 2004, and Zimanyi et al., 2016, and is illustrated in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Loop 1 in class I and II RNRs is the binding site for nucleotides that control the identity of the substrate in the active site.
source: Class I and II RNRs dimerize in anti-parallel orientation at these helices, such that the dimer interface is capped on both ends with a functional insertion known as loop 1 (Figure 1B–C, dark green), which is the binding site for nucleotides that control the identity of the substrate in the active site (Larsson et al., 2004; Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 2004, and Zimanyi et al., 2016, and is illustrated in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The binding of specificity-regulating effectors at loop 1 is coupled to substrate binding via loop 2.
source: The binding of these so-called specificity-regulating effectors is coupled to substrate binding via another insertion known as loop 2 (Figure 1B–C, red) (Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zimanyi et al., 2016, and is illustrated in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Class I and II RNRs share a long β-hairpin motif between the αH helix and βH strand.
source: Class I and II RNRs also share another insertion, a long β-hairpin motif, between the αH helix and βH strand.
evidence: This claim is based on structural observations of class I and II RNRs.

claim: The β-hairpin motif in class I and II RNRs is thought to be important for binding the radical cofactor.
source: Although less is known about the function of this insertion, it is thought to be important for binding the radical cofactor (the entire ferritin subunit in the case of class I RNRs and the AdoCbl cofactor in the case of class II RNRs) (Kang et al., 2020; Sintchak et al., 2002; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2020, Sintchak et al., 2002, and Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: Class III RNRs dimerize at the αA and αB helices such that they are oriented parallel to each other across the interface.
source: Class III RNRs, on the other hand, dimerize at the αA and αB helices such that they are oriented parallel to each other across the interface. This orientation is stabilized by a long helix in place of the loop 1 insertion (Logan et al., 1999; Figure 1D, dark green).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Logan et al., 1999, and is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The parallel orientation of class III RNR dimers is stabilized by a long helix in place of the loop 1 insertion.
source: Class III RNRs, on the other hand, dimerize at the αA and αB helices such that they are oriented parallel to each other across the interface. This orientation is stabilized by a long helix in place of the loop 1 insertion (Logan et al., 1999; Figure 1D, dark green).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Logan et al., 1999, and is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Class III RNRs contain a glycyl radical domain with a zinc finger motif at the C-terminus.
source: Additionally, the class III RNRs contain a glycyl radical domain with a zinc finger motif at the C-terminus.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about class III RNR structure.

claim: The C-termini of class I and II RNRs that have been characterized are unstructured and contain cysteines to re-reduce the active-site cysteines via disulfide exchange.
source: In contrast, the C-termini of class I and II RNRs that have been characterized are unstructured and contain cysteines to re-reduce the active-site cysteines via disulfide exchange (Booker et al., 1994; Mao et al., 1992; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Booker et al., 1994, Mao et al., 1992, and Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: Class I and II RNRs share more structural similarities with each other than they do with class III RNRs.
source: Thus, overall, class I and II RNRs share more structural similarities with each other than they do with class III RNRs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural comparisons described in the preceding text.

claim: Class I RNRs have been proposed to be the most recently evolved class as they require molecular oxygen.
source: Class I RNRs have been proposed to be the most recently evolved class as they require molecular oxygen, which became abundant as the Earth's atmosphere transitioned from anoxic to oxic.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about oxygen requirements and Earth's atmospheric history.

claim: Class III RNRs have been proposed to have emerged before the transition from anoxic to oxic atmosphere as glycyl radicals and [4Fe-4S] clusters are both extremely oxygen-sensitive.
source: In contrast, class III RNRs have been proposed to have emerged before this transition as glycyl radicals and [4Fe-4S] clusters are both extremely oxygen-sensitive (Fontecave et al., 1989) and Fe-S chemistry is thought to have a prebiotic origin (Goldman and Kaçar, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fontecave et al., 1989, and Goldman and Kaçar, 2021.

claim: Fe-S chemistry is thought to have a prebiotic origin.
source: In contrast, class III RNRs have been proposed to have emerged before this transition as glycyl radicals and [4Fe-4S] clusters are both extremely oxygen-sensitive (Fontecave et al., 1989) and Fe-S chemistry is thought to have a prebiotic origin (Goldman and Kaçar, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldman and Kaçar, 2021.

claim: The AdoCbl chemistry used by class II RNRs is neither oxygen-dependent nor especially oxygen-sensitive.
source: The AdoCbl chemistry used by class II RNRs, on the other hand, is neither oxygen-dependent nor especially oxygen-sensitive.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cobalamin chemistry.

claim: Class III RNRs have been proposed to be the most ancient of the RNR family based on the relative oxygen sensitivities and biosynthetic complexities of the different cofactors.
source: Based on the relative oxygen sensitivities and biosynthetic complexities of the different cofactors, class III RNRs have been proposed to be the most ancient of the RNR family (Reichard, 1997; Riera et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reichard, 1997, and Riera et al., 1997.

claim: Cobalamin, AdoMet, and Fe-S clusters have all been proposed to be part of the cofactor set used by the last universal common ancestor.
source: Indeed, cobalamin, AdoMet, and Fe-S clusters have all been proposed to be part of the cofactor set used by the last universal common ancestor (Weiss et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2016.

claim: An alternative model proposes that dimeric class II and III RNRs evolved in parallel from a shared ancestor using class II-like chemistry and that class I RNRs then evolved from class II.
source: It has been proposed in an alternative model that dimeric class II and III RNRs evolved in parallel from a shared ancestor using class II-like chemistry and that class I RNRs then evolved from class II (Lundin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lundin et al., 2015.

claim: The alternative model of RNR evolution was derived from a structure-based phylogenetic network.
source: However, this model was derived from a structure-based phylogenetic network (Bryant and Moulton, 2004), which estimates a phylogeny based on pairwise structural alignment scores rather than evolutionary modelling on protein sequences with well-established amino acid substitution models and statistical frameworks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bryant and Moulton, 2004.

claim: The reconstruction of a large-scale, unifying phylogenetic inference that includes all classes of RNRs has been hindered by the significant computational demand imposed by the high sequence diversity of the extant members of the family.
source: Despite much effort to understand the diversity and evolution of RNRs, the reconstruction of a large-scale, unifying phylogenetic inference that includes all classes of RNRs has been hindered by the significant computational demand imposed by the high sequence diversity of the extant members of the family.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the challenges in RNR phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The study reconstructed the largest RNR phylogeny to-date, consisting of 6779 α sequences, that unifies all classes.
source: In this study, we used the conserved 10-stranded α/β barrel to anchor highly diverged RNR sequences in a structure-based alignment and used maximum-likelihood (ML) inference to reconstruct the largest RNR phylogeny to-date, consisting of 6779 α sequences, that unifies all classes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the study, specifically the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 2.

claim: The comprehensive phylogeny shows the parallel development of three major clades, corresponding to the three known classes.
source: Our comprehensive phylogeny shows the parallel development of three major clades, corresponding to the three known classes, with a small, phylogenetically distinct clade, which we denote as class Ø (for convenience, pronounced 'oh'), placed as an ancestral clade to the class I and II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: A small, phylogenetically distinct clade, denoted as class Ø, is placed as an ancestral clade to the class I and II RNRs.
source: Our comprehensive phylogeny shows the parallel development of three major clades, corresponding to the three known classes, with a small, phylogenetically distinct clade, which we denote as class Ø (for convenience, pronounced 'oh'), placed as an ancestral clade to the class I and II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The class Ø α is the most minimal RNR structurally characterized thus far.
source: Using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), cryogenic-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), and AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021), we show that the class Ø α is the most minimal RNR structurally characterized thus far.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the study, including SAXS, cryo-EM, and AlphaFold2 predictions.

claim: Evo-velocity analysis independently validated the evolutionary model.
source: These observations were corroborated by evo-velocity analysis, an alignment-independent method that employs protein language models to infer sequence fitness and evolutionary trajectories (Hie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis presented in the study, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Class III RNRs diverged early on and evolved independently of class I and II RNRs.
source: Together, our analyses indicate that class III RNRs diverged early on and evolved independently of class I and II RNRs, which diverged from an ancestor shared with the minimal, class Ø RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and evo-velocity analyses presented in the study.

claim: Class I and II RNRs diverged from an ancestor shared with the minimal, class Ø RNRs.
source: Together, our analyses indicate that class III RNRs diverged early on and evolved independently of class I and II RNRs, which diverged from an ancestor shared with the minimal, class Ø RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and evo-velocity analyses presented in the study.

claim: The evolutionary model provides an explanation for the structural similarities of the class I and II RNRs.
source: Our evolutionary model provides an explanation for the structural similarities of the class I and II RNRs and also supports the idea that adaptations to an oxygenated atmosphere appeared earlier than initially thought.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results and structural comparisons.

claim: The evolutionary model supports the idea that adaptations to an oxygenated atmosphere appeared earlier than initially thought.
source: Our evolutionary model provides an explanation for the structural similarities of the class I and II RNRs and also supports the idea that adaptations to an oxygenated atmosphere appeared earlier than initially thought.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: A recently developed workflow uses ensembles of hidden Markov models (HMMs) guided by structural information to build an accurate alignment of 6779 α sequences that spans five PFAM families.
source: To overcome these challenges, we adapted a recently developed workflow (Spence et al., 2021), which uses ensembles of hidden Markov models (HMMs) guided by structural information to build an accurate alignment of 6779 α sequences that spans five PFAM families.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spence et al., 2021, and describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: All reconstructed topologies that converged and failed rejection by the AU-test resolved the three biochemical classes of RNRs as monophyletic lineages.
source: Consistent with our current understanding of RNR evolution, all reconstructed topologies that converged and failed rejection by the AU-test resolved the three biochemical classes of RNRs as monophyletic lineages (Figure 2, blue/yellow/red).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis and statistical testing presented in the study.

claim: There is strong support for classes I and II diverging from a single common ancestor that shared an ancestor with the class III RNRs.
source: Additionally, we find strong support for classes I and II diverging from a single common ancestor that shared an ancestor with the class III RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: A novel clade of α sequences diverged from the last common ancestor (LCA) of classes I and II, denoted as the class Ø clade.
source: We identified a novel clade of α sequences that diverged from the last common ancestor (LCA) of classes I and II, which we denote as the class Ø clade (Figure 2, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The branch that separates the LCA of classes Ø, I, II from class III is the midpoint of the phylogeny.
source: In the topology with the best statistical support, the branch that separates the LCA of classes Ø, I, II from class III is the midpoint of the phylogeny.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Rooting on the midpoint branch places class III as the most ancestral, followed by the emergence of the LCA of classes Ø, I, II and the subsequent divergence of classes I and II.
source: Rooting on this branch places class III as the most ancestral, followed by the emergence of the LCA of classes Ø, I, II and the subsequent divergence of classes I and II.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic analysis and midpoint rooting.

claim: Evo-velocity analysis is a machine-learning analysis based on the principles of natural language processing (NLP).
source: Evo-velocity is a machine-learning analysis based on the principles of natural language processing (NLP) (Hie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hie et al., 2022.

claim: ESM-1b is a >650,000,000 parameter NLP model trained on UniProt50 amino acid sequences.
source: NLP models such as ESM-1b, a >650,000,000 parameter NLP model trained on UniProt50 amino acid sequences (Rives et al., 2021), can embed query sequences in a high-dimensional space where likelihoods can be numerically computed as proxy fitness scores on a graph network.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rives et al., 2021.

claim: The ESM-1b embedded RNR graph network shares many common topological features with the full family phylogeny.
source: When projected onto a two-dimensional basis (see Methods), the ESM-1b embedded RNR graph network (Figure 3) shares many common topological features with the full family phylogeny (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Figure 3 and Figure 2.

claim: Class III RNRs belong to a diverged cluster of sequences that have evolved independently of class I and II sequences.
source: Class III RNRs (Figure 3A, red) belong to a diverged cluster of sequences that have evolved independently of class I and II sequences (Figure 3A, blue/yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Classes I and II are joined over the same sequence space, indicating a common recent ancestor.
source: Conversely, classes I and II are joined over the same sequence space, indicating a common recent ancestor.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The class Ø sequences occupy the interface between classes I and II, consistent with their phylogenetic placement as ancestral to the class I/II lineage.
source: The class Ø sequences occupy the interface between classes I and II (Figure 3A, green), consistent with their phylogenetic placement as ancestral to the class I/II lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Evo-velocity analysis identified multiple roots in the RNR family.
source: Evo-velocity analysis also identified multiple roots in the RNR family (Figure 3B, dark purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The multiple roots identified by evo-velocity analysis belong to each of the major lineages, signifying independent evolution down distinct trajectories.
source: The multiple roots belong to each of the major lineages, signifying independent evolution down distinct trajectories.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pseudotime velocity clearly captures the interface of class I and II sequences (including class Ø) as the most ancestral within that lineage.
source: However, pseudotime velocity, a proxy for phylogenetic depth (Haghverdi et al., 2016), clearly captures the interface of class I and II sequences (including class Ø) as the most ancestral within that lineage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evo-velocity analysis shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Haghverdi et al., 2016.

claim: The class Ø clade consists of RNRs from both bacteria and phages, many of which are phototrophs.
source: The class Ø clade consists of RNRs from both bacteria and phages, many of which are phototrophs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the taxonomic analysis of the class Ø clade shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nearly half of the sequences in the class Ø clade were obtained from cyanophages or uncultured phages.
source: Nearly half of the sequences in the clade were obtained from cyanophages (Figure 4A, bolded species) or uncultured phages, while the remainder were obtained from marine bacteria, including those collected in the Tara Oceans Expedition (Tully et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the taxonomic analysis shown in Figure 4A and a citation to Tully et al., 2018.

claim: A BLAST search of photosynthetic genes (psbA and psbD) against the genomes of the 35 bacteria and phages in the class Ø clade yielded 11 hits.
source: Performing a BLAST search of photosynthetic genes, such as psbA and psbD, against the genomes (of which many are incomplete) of the 35 bacteria and phages listed in the clade yielded 11 hits (Figure 4A, species in green).
evidence: This claim is supported by the BLAST search results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All completely sequenced operons with a class Ø RNR α gene contain a small ferritin-like gene immediately downstream.
source: Additionally, we find that all completely sequenced operons with a class Ø RNR α gene (24/35 in Figure 4A) contain a small ferritin-like gene (annotated with InterPro family number for the ferritin-like superfamily IPR009078) immediately downstream (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and thus, we find that this feature is not exclusive to cyanophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An all-vs.-all pBLAST search of every class Ø sequence against all class I sequences detects poor homology (E-value > 0.05).
source: Interestingly, an all-vs.-all pBLAST search of every class Ø sequence against all class I sequences in our phylogeny detects poor homology (E-value > 0.05) (Figure 4B, blue), while querying class Ø RNRs against class II returns hundreds of significant hits (E-value < 1E-10) (Figure 4B, yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by the BLAST search results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Querying class Ø RNRs against class II returns hundreds of significant hits (E-value < 1E-10).
source: Interestingly, an all-vs.-all pBLAST search of every class Ø sequence against all class I sequences in our phylogeny detects poor homology (E-value > 0.05) (Figure 4B, blue), while querying class Ø RNRs against class II returns hundreds of significant hits (E-value < 1E-10) (Figure 4B, yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by the BLAST search results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: By sequence homology, class Ø RNRs appear to be more class II like despite being associated with a ferritin-like gene that is reminiscent of class I RNRs.
source: Thus, by sequence homology, class Ø RNRs appear to be more class II like despite being associated with a ferritin-like gene that is reminiscent of class I RNRs, which supports the phylogenetic results indicting they are a distinct class.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the BLAST search results and genomic analysis.

claim: The class Ø lineage consists of α sequences with an average length of 412 amino acids.
source: The class Ø lineage consists of α sequences with an average length of 412 amino acids, which are significantly shorter than those of the class Id catalytic subunit that were previously described as having a minimal architecture with a median length of 565 amino acids (Rose et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence length analysis and a citation to Rose et al., 2019.

claim: Class Ø α sequences are significantly shorter than those of the class Id catalytic subunit that were previously described as having a minimal architecture with a median length of 565 amino acids.
source: The class Ø lineage consists of α sequences with an average length of 412 amino acids, which are significantly shorter than those of the class Id catalytic subunit that were previously described as having a minimal architecture with a median length of 565 amino acids (Rose et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence length analysis and a citation to Rose et al., 2019.

claim: Class Ø sequences all lack an ~100-residue ATP-cone motif at the N-terminus.
source: Like the class Id α sequences, the class Ø sequences all lack an ~100-residue ATP-cone motif at the N-terminus, which is used for allosteric regulation of overall activity in many other RNRs (Meisburger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and a citation to Meisburger et al., 2017.

claim: The class Ø C-terminus contains a double cysteine motif, which is likely used for reducing a pair of active-site cysteines that are oxidized following every turnover.
source: Additionally, the class Ø C-terminus contains a double cysteine motif, which is likely used for reducing a pair of active-site cysteines that are oxidized following every turnover.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence analysis and knowledge of RNR catalytic mechanisms.

claim: Of the 24 class Ø sequences that are complete at the C-terminus, 10 contain a CXXC motif and 14 contain a CXC motif.
source: Of the 24 class Ø sequences that are complete at the C-terminus, 10 contain a CXXC motif and 14 contain a CXC motif (where aspartic acid is the most common middle amino acid).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of class Ø RNRs.

claim: The C-terminal CXXC motif is a common feature of class I RNRs (found in 1737 of 2022 class I sequences in the dataset).
source: The C-terminal CXXC motif is a common feature of class I RNRs (found in 1737 of 2022 class I sequences in our dataset), but the CXC motif is rare among both class I and II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of class I RNRs in the dataset.

claim: The CXC motif is rare among both class I and II RNRs.
source: The C-terminal CXXC motif is a common feature of class I RNRs (found in 1737 of 2022 class I sequences in our dataset), but the CXC motif is rare among both class I and II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of class I and II RNRs in the dataset.

claim: Only seven class I sequences and one class II sequence in the dataset appear to have a CXC motif.
source: Only seven class I sequences and one class II sequence in our dataset appear to have a CXC motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of the dataset.

claim: The CXXC-containing sequences are most ancestral within the class Ø clade, while the more recently evolved sequences have the CXC motif.
source: Interestingly, the CXXC-containing sequences are most ancestral within the class Ø clade, while the more recently evolved sequences have the CXC motif.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic analysis of class Ø sequences.

claim: In the absence of nucleotides, SAXS profiles of the S-CBP4 α subunit are consistent with a monomer-dimer equilibrium.
source: In the absence of nucleotides, our SAXS profiles are consistent with a monomer-dimer equilibrium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) where the S-CBP4 α subunit is predominantly monomeric at low protein concentrations (≤4 μM).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The S-CBP4 α subunit is predominantly monomeric at low protein concentrations (≤4 μM).
source: In the absence of nucleotides, our SAXS profiles are consistent with a monomer-dimer equilibrium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) where the S-CBP4 α subunit is predominantly monomeric at low protein concentrations (≤4 μM).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of substrate (GDP) does not shift the monomer-dimer equilibrium of the S-CBP4 α subunit.
source: Addition of substrate (guanosine diphosphate [GDP]) does not shift this equilibrium, but the presence of the corresponding specificity effector (thymidine triphosphate [TTP]), strongly favors dimerization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of the specificity effector TTP strongly favors dimerization of the S-CBP4 α subunit.
source: Addition of substrate (guanosine diphosphate [GDP]) does not shift this equilibrium, but the presence of the corresponding specificity effector (thymidine triphosphate [TTP]), strongly favors dimerization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A cryo-EM map of the S-CBP4 α2 dimer was obtained to 3.46 Å resolution (FSC = 0.143).
source: Using solution conditions that saturate nucleotide binding (200 μM TTP, 200 μM GDP), we obtained a cryo-EM map of the S-CBP4 α2 dimer to 3.46 Å resolution (Fourier shell correlation [FSC] = 0.143) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: An atomic model (residues 22–426 out of 470) was refined against the cryo-EM map using an AlphaFold2 prediction as the starting model.
source: An atomic model (residues 22–426 out of 470) was refined against the cryo-EM map using an AlphaFold2 prediction as the starting model (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model refinement procedure described in the Methods.

claim: The final refined model was highly similar to the starting AlphaFold2 model with a root mean square deviation (all-atom RMSD) of 1.44 Å.
source: The final refined model was highly similar to the starting model with a root mean square deviation (all-atom RMSD) of 1.44 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model refinement statistics.

claim: The S-CBP4 α subunit displays the most minimal RNR architecture discovered to-date with few insertions about the catalytic barrel.
source: Overall, the S-CBP4 α subunit displays the most minimal RNR architecture discovered to-date with few insertions about the catalytic barrel (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The minimal set of insertions in the S-CBP4 α subunit includes traits shared by class I and II RNRs, such as loop 1.
source: The minimal set of insertions includes traits shared by class I and II RNRs, such as loop 1, where we find cryo-EM density for bound TTP (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cryo-EM density for bound TTP was found at loop 1 of the S-CBP4 α subunit.
source: The minimal set of insertions includes traits shared by class I and II RNRs, such as loop 1, where we find cryo-EM density for bound TTP (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The S-CBP4 α subunit contains a long β-hairpin following the βH strand of the catalytic barrel.
source: Additionally, the S-CBP4 α subunit contains a long β-hairpin following the βH strand of the catalytic barrel that in class II RNRs is thought to be important for cofactor binding (Sintchak et al., 2002) and in class I RNRs is thought to be important for interactions with the β subunit (Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and citations to Sintchak et al., 2002, and Kang et al., 2020.

claim: Two consecutive tyrosine residues (Y420 and Y421) on βJ of the S-CBP4 α subunit are well resolved and stacked adjacent to the catalytic cysteine (C185) at the tip of finger loop.
source: Although we do not observe density for the C-terminus past the βJ strand of the catalytic barrel, two consecutive tyrosine residues (Y420 and Y421) on βJ are well resolved and stacked adjacent to the catalytic cysteine (C185) at the tip of finger loop (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In class I RNRs, the stacked arrangement of the tyrosine dyad is required for long-range proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) between the β subunit and the catalytic cysteine.
source: In class I RNRs, this stacked arrangement of the tyrosine dyad is required for long-range proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) between the β subunit and the catalytic cysteine (Greene et al., 2017; Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greene et al., 2017, and is illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: In class II RNRs, the space between the βJ strand and the finger-loop cysteine forms a pocket to accommodate the adenosyl group of the cobalamin cofactor.
source: By comparison, inspection of existing structures (Larsson et al., 2010; Sintchak et al., 2002) suggests that in class II RNRs, the space between the βJ strand and the finger-loop cysteine forms a pocket to accommodate the adenosyl group of the cobalamin cofactor (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 2010, and Sintchak et al., 2002, and is illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: A disulfide was observed between active-site cysteines (C30 and C196) in the S-CBP4 α subunit.
source: Finally, we observe a disulfide between active-site cysteines (C30 and C196) that in class I and II RNRs serve as reducing equivalents during nucleotide reduction (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The active-site cysteines C30 and C196 in class I and II RNRs serve as reducing equivalents during nucleotide reduction.
source: Finally, we observe a disulfide between active-site cysteines (C30 and C196) that in class I and II RNRs serve as reducing equivalents during nucleotide reduction (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about RNR catalytic mechanisms.

claim: Class Ø ferritin-like proteins are significantly shorter (average length of 240 amino acids) than those of bona fide class I β subunits (average length of 346 amino acids).
source: Although the class Ø α subunit contains a tyrosine dyad poised for PCET like class I α subunits, the class Ø ferritin-like sequences are significantly shorter (average length of 240 amino acids) than those of bona fide class I β subunits (average length of 346 amino acids).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence length analysis.

claim: Querying each complete class Ø ferritin-like sequence returns only a single homologous sequence over the whole length of the alignment when searched against PFAM families PF00210 and PF00268.
source: Querying each complete class Ø ferritin-like sequence returns only a single homologous sequence over the whole length of the alignment (all hits E-value > 1E-4, excluding one) when searched against PFAM families PF00210 (ferritin-like proteins, 17,981 entries) and PF00268 (class I RNR β subunit, 9898 entries).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLAST search results against PFAM families.

claim: Based on AlphaFold2, class Ø ferritin-like proteins resemble class I β subunits with shorter insertions and termini.
source: However, based on AlphaFold2, which detects more than sequence homology, class Ø ferritin-like proteins resemble class I β subunits with shorter insertions and termini (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A-D.

claim: Class Ø ferritin-like proteins are predicted to contain a core ferritin fold consisting of two helix-turn-helices.
source: As in class I β subunits, the class Ø proteins are predicted to contain a core ferritin fold consisting of two helix-turn-helices (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A and C, red/pink and yellow/green), each contributing an E/D+EXXH metal-binding motif (Ruskoski and Boal, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A and C, and a citation to Ruskoski and Boal, 2021.

claim: Class Ø ferritin-like proteins contain a redox-inert residue (Phe or Leu) at the site where most class I β sequences have a tyrosine serving as the site of the radical.
source: Additionally, while most class I β sequences have a tyrosine serving as the site of the radical downstream of the first metal-binding motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), class Ø ferritin-like proteins contain a redox-inert residue (Phe or Leu) at this site, much like class Ic RNRs (Bollinger et al., 2008; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Figure 4—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6E and citations to Bollinger et al., 2008, and Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011.

claim: Class Ø ferritin-like sequences contain a C-terminal tyrosine which in class I RNRs is involved in inter-subunit radical transfer.
source: Class Ø ferritin-like sequences also contain a C-terminal tyrosine (Y239 in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A), which in class I RNRs is involved in inter-subunit radical transfer (Y356 in Figure 4—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A and C.

claim: The C-termini of the class Ø ferritin-like proteins are unusually short, terminating at the residue downstream from the C-terminal tyrosine.
source: However, the C-termini of the class Ø ferritin-like proteins are unusually short, terminating at the residue downstream from this tyrosine, and lack the ~10-residue extension that class I β subunits use for binding to the α subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of class Ø ferritin-like proteins.

claim: The class Ø ferritin-like proteins lack the ~10-residue extension that class I β subunits use for binding to the α subunit.
source: However, the C-termini of the class Ø ferritin-like proteins are unusually short, terminating at the residue downstream from this tyrosine, and lack the ~10-residue extension that class I β subunits use for binding to the α subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of class Ø ferritin-like proteins.

claim: The class Ø ferritin-like proteins are likely to use a similar radical-generating mechanism as class I β subunits.
source: Thus, although the class Ø ferritin-like proteins are likely to use a similar radical-generating mechanism as class I β subunits, they may interact with the α subunit in a different manner to enable PCET.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The class Ø ferritin-like proteins may interact with the α subunit in a different manner to enable PCET.
source: Thus, although the class Ø ferritin-like proteins are likely to use a similar radical-generating mechanism as class I β subunits, they may interact with the α subunit in a different manner to enable PCET.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from structural differences.

claim: The class Ø ferritin-like proteins can be unstable in the absence of metals.
source: However, ongoing biochemical work to confirm this has thus far been non-trivial as the class Ø ferritin-like proteins can be unstable in the absence of metals, most likely because of their small size.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations during biochemical characterization attempts.

claim: The class Ø α structure illustrates how the class I and II RNRs may have inherited shared traits from a common ancestor.
source: Regardless, the class Ø α structure illustrates how the class I and II RNRs may have inherited shared traits from a common ancestor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural analysis of class Ø RNRs.

claim: Prior to this work, phylogenetic inference on RNRs had only been performed on a very small scale.
source: Thus, although various models for RNR evolution have been proposed by biochemical reasoning (e.g., based on the availabilities and oxygen sensitivities of the cofactors), prior to our work, phylogenetic inference had only been performed on a very small scale.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of the literature on RNR phylogenetics.

claim: Early phylogenetic studies on RNRs included an inference of eight class II sequences performed with Clustal W.
source: Early studies included an inference of eight class II sequences (Jordan et al., 1997) performed with Clustal W (Thompson et al., 1994) and an inference with a dataset of 96 class I, II, and III sequences (Torrents et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jordan et al., 1997, and Thompson et al., 1994.

claim: Torrents and co-workers used a neighbor-joining (NJ) algorithm to build a tree using a Poisson model for a dataset of 96 class I, II, and III sequences.
source: In the latter study, Torrents and co-workers used a neighbor-joining (NJ) algorithm to build a tree using a Poisson model, which assumes that all amino acids have equal probability of change (Torrents et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Torrents et al., 2002.

claim: The NJ approach differs significantly from modern methods of tree inference in which the tree topology is determined by the sequence evolution model itself.
source: This approach differs significantly from modern methods of tree inference in which the tree topology is determined by the sequence evolution model itself (Minh et al., 2020) often in replicate.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Minh et al., 2020.

claim: The dataset used by Torrents et al. lacked class Ø sequences, monomeric class II sequences, as well as many subclasses of the class I sequences.
source: Furthermore, the sequence availability at the time was too sparse to capture the true diversity of the RNR family, and the dataset lacked class Ø sequences, monomeric class II sequences, as well as many subclasses of the class I sequences.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the Torrents et al. dataset with the current study's dataset.

claim: Small-scale phylogenetic inferences have been performed on subsets of the RNR family with datasets ranging between 10s and 100s of sequences in size.
source: Since then, small-scale inferences have been performed on subsets of the RNR family on either the α or β subunit with datasets ranging between 10s and 100s of sequences in size (Dwivedi et al., 2013; Lundin et al., 2010; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2019; Rozman-Grinberg et al., 2018; Sakowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The work of Lundin and co-workers has been the most comprehensive with respect to consideration of the different RNR classes.
source: Among these, the work of Lundin and co-workers has been the most comprehensive with respect to consideration of the different RNR classes (Lundin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lundin et al., 2010.

claim: A structure-based phylogenetic network was constructed via an NJ algorithm, where the distance between two sequences was estimated by pairwise structural alignment scores.
source: In its place, a structure-based phylogenetic network was constructed via an NJ algorithm, where the distance between two sequences was estimated by pairwise structural alignment scores (Lundin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lundin et al., 2015.

claim: Under the assumption that the structure-based phylogenetic network estimates a phylogenetic tree, it was proposed that the class I RNRs emerged from the dimeric class II RNRs.
source: Under the assumption that this network estimates a phylogenetic tree, different possible roots were considered, and although none led to monophyly of the RNR classes, it was proposed that the class I RNRs emerged from the dimeric class II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the structure-based phylogenetic network by Lundin et al., 2015.

claim: The study succeeded in performing a large-scale phylogenetic reconstruction of the entire, highly diverse RNR family for the first time by using structural information to aid the sequence alignment procedure.
source: In this study, we succeeded in performing a large-scale phylogenetic reconstruction of the entire, highly diverse RNR family for the first time by using structural information to aid the sequence alignment procedure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methodology and results presented in the study.

claim: ML inference was performed using two different amino acid replacement matrices in replicate (10 trees for each model).
source: To test for alternative hypotheses, we performed ML inference using two different amino acid replacement matrices in replicate (10 trees for each model) and repeated the inference with a different sequence redundancy threshold to test for the effect of taxon sampling on tree topology and evolutionary conclusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methodology described in the study.

claim: The inference was repeated with a different sequence redundancy threshold to test for the effect of taxon sampling on tree topology and evolutionary conclusions.
source: To test for alternative hypotheses, we performed ML inference using two different amino acid replacement matrices in replicate (10 trees for each model) and repeated the inference with a different sequence redundancy threshold to test for the effect of taxon sampling on tree topology and evolutionary conclusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methodology described in the study.

claim: Key bifurcations in the phylogeny featured high branch supports and reproducibility in replicate tree inferences.
source: Key bifurcations featured high branch supports and reproducibility in replicate tree inferences, allowing us to make robust interpretations, which were further supported by evo-velocity analysis, a recently introduced method that is independent of multiple sequence alignments (Hie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis results and a citation to Hie et al., 2022.

claim: The unified RNR phylogeny supports the evolution of three major, monophyletic clades corresponding to the three biochemically known classes as well as a new phylogenetic clade, class Ø.
source: In contrast to previously proposed models (Lundin et al., 2015), our unified RNR phylogeny supports the evolution of three major, monophyletic clades corresponding to the three biochemically known classes as well as a new phylogenetic clade, which we denoted as class Ø.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: The bioinformatic analyses support an evolutionary trajectory in which the O2-sensitive class III RNRs are the earliest to diverge.
source: Together, our bioinformatic analyses support an evolutionary trajectory in which the O2-sensitive class III RNRs are the earliest to diverge, and the class Ø clade shares an ancestor with the LCA of the O2-dependent class I and O2-tolerant class II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and evo-velocity analyses presented in the study.

claim: The class Ø clade shares an ancestor with the LCA of the O2-dependent class I and O2-tolerant class II RNRs.
source: Together, our bioinformatic analyses support an evolutionary trajectory in which the O2-sensitive class III RNRs are the earliest to diverge, and the class Ø clade shares an ancestor with the LCA of the O2-dependent class I and O2-tolerant class II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and evo-velocity analyses presented in the study.

claim: The phylogeny revealed the novel class Ø clade, which is exclusively associated with marine microbes, such as cyanophages and photosynthetic bacteria.
source: Most notably, our phylogeny revealed the novel class Ø clade, which is exclusively (among characterized organisms) associated with marine microbes, such as cyanophages and photosynthetic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and taxonomic analyses presented in the study.

claim: The class Ø α subunit shares significant sequence homology with class II sequences.
source: Bioinformatically, we showed that the class Ø α subunit shares significant sequence homology with class II sequences, while also containing in its gene neighborhood a gene for a ferritin-like protein that resembles the class I β subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the BLAST search results presented in the study.

claim: The class Ø α subunit contains in its gene neighborhood a gene for a ferritin-like protein that resembles the class I β subunit.
source: Bioinformatically, we showed that the class Ø α subunit shares significant sequence homology with class II sequences, while also containing in its gene neighborhood a gene for a ferritin-like protein that resembles the class I β subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic and structural analyses presented in the study.

claim: The class Ø α subunit defines the minimum set of features shared by class I and II RNRs, including the orientation of the two monomers in the dimer, specificity site at loop 1, and the β-hairpin.
source: Structurally, we further showed that the class Ø α subunit defines the minimum set of features shared by class I and II RNRs, including the orientation of the two monomers in the dimer, specificity site at loop 1, and the β-hairpin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis presented in the study.

claim: It was previously hypothesized that the LCA of RNRs may have possessed class II-like biochemistry based on the Precambrian bioavailabilities of iron and cobalt and the abiotic synthesis of porphyrin rings.
source: It was previously hypothesized that the LCA of RNRs may have possessed class II-like biochemistry based on the Precambrian bioavailabilities of iron and cobalt and the abiotic synthesis of porphyrin rings (Lundin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lundin et al., 2015.

claim: The phylogeny suggests that a class II-like enzyme resembling the extant class Ø sequences recruited a ferritin-like protein into the catalytic machinery, before diverging into class I RNRs and class II RNRs.
source: An alternative hypothesis is supported by our phylogeny, which places the class I mechanism as ancestral to, or having diverged in parallel with, that of class II. Although we cannot classify the mechanism of radical generation in the class Ø RNRs in the absence of biochemical data, our phylogeny suggests that a class II-like enzyme resembling the extant class Ø sequences recruited a ferritin-like protein into the catalytic machinery, before diverging into class I RNRs (which retained a ferritin subunit for catalysis) and class II RNRs (which specialized in cobalamin usage).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results.

claim: The usage of a ferritin-like protein in class Ø RNRs is supported by the observation of a stacked YY dyad in the active site of the cryo-EM structure.
source: The usage of a ferritin-like protein in class Ø RNRs is supported by the observation of a stacked YY dyad in the active site of our cryo-EM structure, which suggests that long-range radical transfer is an important component of catalysis in these enzymes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The stacked YY dyad in the active site of the class Ø cryo-EM structure suggests that long-range radical transfer is an important component of catalysis in these enzymes.
source: The usage of a ferritin-like protein in class Ø RNRs is supported by the observation of a stacked YY dyad in the active site of our cryo-EM structure, which suggests that long-range radical transfer is an important component of catalysis in these enzymes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cryo-EM structure and knowledge of PCET mechanisms.

claim: The short C-terminus of the class Ø ferritins and the prevalence of the CXC motif in the α C-terminus suggest that there are key differences with the class I and II RNRs.
source: However, the short C-terminus of the class Ø ferritins and the prevalence of the CXC motif in the α C-terminus suggest that there are key differences with the class I and II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence and structural analysis.

claim: The LCA of the RNR catalytic subunit likely shared the most biochemical resemblance to extant class III RNRs.
source: Based on our results, we present the following model for the evolution of the RNR family. The LCA of the RNR catalytic subunit likely shared the most biochemical resemblance to extant class III RNRs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results.

claim: Increasing oxygen availability selected for the divergence of the RNR family into the anaerobic LCA of class III and the oxygen-tolerant LCA of classes Ø–II.
source: Increasing oxygen availability selected for the divergence of the RNR family into the anaerobic LCA of class III and the oxygen-tolerant LCA of classes Ø–II, from which the minimal class Ø RNRs diverged.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Class I and II RNRs sharing an ancestor would suggest that multiple strategies to adapt to the presence of oxygen evolved in parallel, rather than sequentially.
source: Class I and II RNRs sharing an ancestor would suggest that multiple strategies to adapt to the presence of oxygen evolved in parallel, rather than sequentially.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results.

claim: Sequences from the earliest diverging cyanobacterium, Gloeobacter, are found near the root of the class II clade in the phylogeny.
source: Interestingly, we find sequences from the earliest diverging cyanobacterium, Gloeobacter, near the root of the class II clade in our phylogeny.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Gloeobacter are notable for lacking thylakoid membranes and have been called 'the missing link' between anoxic photosynthesis and oxygenic photosynthesis.
source: Gloeobacter are notable for lacking thylakoid membranes and have been called 'the missing link' between anoxic photosynthesis, which involves Fe-S chemistry, and oxygenic photosynthesis (Nakamura et al., 2003; Saw et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2003, and Saw et al., 2013.

claim: It is possible that class II RNRs evolved well before the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE).
source: Thus, along with the emergence of cyanobacteria (Schirrmeister et al., 2013), it is possible that class II RNRs evolved well before the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the phylogenetic results and a citation to Schirrmeister et al., 2013.

claim: If class II RNRs evolved before the GOE, this would imply that class I RNRs also emerged before the Earth's atmosphere became permanently oxidizing.
source: If so, this would imply that class I RNRs also emerged before the Earth's atmosphere became permanently oxidizing.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on logical inference from the previous claim.

claim: Recent work suggests that oxygen availability was sufficient for the birth of O2-producing and O2-utilizing enzymes to occur well before the geochemically defined GOE.
source: In fact, recent work suggests that oxygen availability was sufficient for the birth of O2-producing and O2-utilizing enzymes to occur well before the geochemically defined GOE (Jabłońska and Tawfik, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jabłońska and Tawfik, 2021.

claim: The evolutionary model could explain how O2-dependent class I RNRs can share an ancestor with class II RNRs.
source: Such an evolutionary model could explain how O2-dependent class I RNRs can share an ancestor with class II RNRs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the evolutionary model and the timing of oxygen availability.

claim: It is especially intriguing that class Ø RNRs are associated with cyanophages and photosynthetic bacteria.
source: In this respect, it is especially intriguing that class Ø RNRs are associated with cyanophages and photosynthetic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is based on the taxonomic analysis of class Ø RNRs and its implications for the evolutionary model.

claim: Biochemical studies of the class Ø clade are expected to provide insight into how an ancestral radical-generating mechanism may have diverged into class I and II mechanisms.
source: We expect biochemical studies of the class Ø clade to provide insight into how an ancestral radical-generating mechanism may have diverged into class I and II mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the expected outcomes of future research.

claim: By analyzing the extensions and insertions about the catalytic barrel, greater understanding of how allosteric and catalytic mechanisms evolved within the RNR family is anticipated.
source: We also anticipate that by analyzing the extensions and insertions about the catalytic barrel, we will gain a greater understanding of how allosteric and catalytic mechanisms evolved within the RNR family.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the expected outcomes of future research.

claim: With a phylogenetic inference, it is conceivable that ancestral sequences can be reconstructed to gain detailed insight into evolutionary trajectories.
source: Finally, with a phylogenetic inference, it is conceivable that we will be able to reconstruct ancestral sequences and gain detailed insight into evolutionary trajectories.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the potential applications of the phylogenetic inference.

claim: The unifying RNR phylogeny will guide future studies to fill important gaps in the understanding of this family of complex enzymes.
source: In all, our unifying RNR phylogeny will guide future studies to fill important gaps in our ever-evolving understanding of this family of complex enzymes.
evidence: This claim is based on the expected impact of the phylogenetic inference on future research.
